# Using USACO Guide and CSES for DSA and Coding Interview Prep

**Source:** https://www.instagram.com/reel/DeJKcDqE2q3/ · **Type:** Reel · **Author:** level5esper · **Saved:** 2026-10-06

**Why I saved it:** DSA

## Summary

USACO Guide is a free, structured platform for mastering data structures and algorithms originally created for competitive programming contestants. Its curriculum, along with standard problems from platforms like CSES, maps directly to common LeetCode patterns and offers an organized roadmap for technical interview preparation.

## Transcript and on-screen text

What is USACO Guide? Do you know what USACO Guide is? It's a free site that teaches you DSA in order, and it explains each topic before you touch the problems. Introduction to Prefix Sums. Computing range sum queries in constant time over a fixed 1D array. It has high-quality written solutions, and again, reading an editorial has plenty of benefits over watching someone else think through a video solution. Our Mission: The USACO supports computing education in the USA and worldwide by identifying, motivating, and training high-school computing students at all levels. It's aimed at high schoolers doing USACO, so it's not meant to be hard. And if you think competitive programming doesn't help in interviews, well, a lot of the guide's problems are literally LeetCode problems with a different name: Counting Rooms is 200. Number of Islands, Minimizing Coins is 322. Coin Change, Static Range Sum Queries is 303. Range Sum Query - Immutable. USACO Guide is community-managed and written by top USACO contestants, including Benjamin Qi, who won the IOI twice and worked at Citadel Securities and now at Anthropic. There's also many strong contestants, like William Lin, who's pretty much LGM, perfect score in IOI, and had a couple famous YouTube videos. The topics are more granular. For example, backtracking is just one section of its Complete Search with Recursion module, right after subsets and permutations. Each module lists its prerequisites, and the ones you can skip say optional in the title, like Hashmaps in Gold. It follows USACO's four divisions. Bronze is the basics, like complete search, sorting, and your first graphs. Then Silver adds prefix sums, binary search, and graph traversal. Gold even gives dynamic programming separate modules, like knapsack, bitmasks, and trees, and Platinum is probably stuff you don't have to worry about. Every module explains the idea with code in C++, Java, and Python, and then gives you practice problems. And lots of them have a written solution that explains why it works. Do the starred problems first, because the guide recommends those. Feel free to skip hard problems, and I wouldn't worry about solving problems in order. For interviews, I'd do Bronze and Silver, then the dynamic programming and graph modules in Gold. If Gold is too hard, do the dynamic programming and graph sections on CSES first, since they're short standard problems like counting coin combinations.
